Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:

  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

 "path": "memory/task-f94a3e13.md",
 "content": "# Continual-ARC task-f94a3e13: paired bands across a separator

Observed demonstration: input is a grid with a full-height vertical separator column (color 4 in the demo; 6 in the test). Nonzero cells occur in equal-width bands to the left and right of the separator, with distinct colors for the bands. Output has the same number of rows and one column per position in either band. For each row and band-position k, output[row][k] = 2 iff the corresponding left and right cells are both nonzero; otherwise output[row][k] = 0. Correspondence is same offset from the outer left/right edges (equivalently, left band column k paired with right band column k, moving away from separator in the shown cases). Ignore the separator and original colors. 

Demonstration: 17x5, separator at col 2, bands width 2. Output 17x2 marks simultaneous occupied pairs. Test: 20x9, separator at col 4, bands width 4, output 20x4.

Important: learned from the solved instance after one incorrect guess. For recurring instances, identify the separator and compare occupancy pairwise across it; do not merely copy one side's pattern."
